flashcards.q: What's the correct diagnostic order: kubectl logs or kubectl describe pod first?
flashcards.a: describe pod first — its Events and Last State tell you which failure bucket you're in (pull failure, crash, scheduling, eviction). logs is only useful once a container has actually run, and is structurally useless for ImagePullBackOff and most Pending cases.

flashcards.q: CrashLoopBackOff exponential backoff schedule and reset condition?
flashcards.a: 10s, 20s, 40s, 80s, 160s, capped at 300s (5 min). Resets after the container stays up 10 minutes straight.

flashcards.q: What does exit code 137 mean, and is it always OOMKilled?
flashcards.a: 137 = 128+9 = killed by SIGKILL. Often OOMKilled but not always (any external SIGKILL produces it) — confirm via 'Reason: OOMKilled' in describe pod's Last State block, not the exit code alone.

flashcards.q: Why does kubectl logs show nothing for an ImagePullBackOff pod?
flashcards.a: No container has ever started — the failure happens entirely during image pull, before the runtime creates any container. Diagnose from kubectl describe pod's Events instead.

flashcards.q: OOMKilled vs Evicted — what's the mechanical difference?
flashcards.a: OOMKilled: kernel's cgroup OOM killer defends that container's own memory cgroup, immediate SIGKILL, exit 137. Evicted: kubelet proactively kills pods to defend the whole NODE under memory/disk/PID pressure, in QoS order (BestEffort first).
memory.available: 100Mi, nodefs.available: 10%, imagefs.available: 15%, nodefs.inodesFree: 5%, imagefs.inodesFree: 5%. Hard thresholds evict immediately, no grace period.

flashcards.q: A JVM service keeps getting OOMKilled even though heap usage looks fine. Likely cause?
flashcards.a: -Xmx set too close to the container's memory limit, leaving no headroom for off-heap usage (metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers) which still counts against the cgroup limit.

flashcards.q: What's the real mechanism behind the well-known '5 second Kubernetes DNS delay'?
flashcards.a: A kernel-level conntrack race when two UDP DNS queries (typically simultaneous A/AAAA) go out from the same source port near-simultaneously, causing one to be dropped; the resolver waits out its full timeout (~5s). Restarting CoreDNS does not fix it — it's not a CoreDNS bug.

flashcards.q: What does ndots:5 (Kubernetes pod DNS default) actually cause?
flashcards.a: Any queried name with fewer than 5 dots gets the cluster's search domains tried first, so external calls like api.stripe.com pay for up to 4-5 wasted NXDOMAIN queries before the absolute name finally succeeds — a steady latency tax, distinct from the conntrack race.

flashcards.q: What does kubectl debug --target=<container> actually do, and since when is it GA?
flashcards.a: Injects a temporary ephemeral container into a running pod, sharing its network namespace and (with --target) the target container's process namespace, without modifying the pod spec or restarting. GA since Kubernetes 1.25; works against distroless/shell-less images.

flashcards.q: A wave of Evicted pods appears on a node but the evicted pods' own memory usage is unremarkable. What's the likely cause?
flashcards.a: Disk pressure (nodefs/imagefs), often from an unrelated high-volume logger filling node disk — the 'innocent bystander' pattern. Eviction removes pods in QoS order regardless of whether they caused the disk usage.

flashcards.q: A pod is Pending with '0/12 nodes are available: 12 Insufficient memory' and Cluster Autoscaler is healthy. First move?
flashcards.a: Check kube-system events for an autoscaler scale-up event referencing the pod — if present, it's just provisioning latency (4-8 min for classic Cluster Autoscaler); if absent, the request likely exceeds any available node group's instance type and needs resizing, not patience.
